lesson.title: Deepfakes and AI-made content
lesson.subtitle: Why your eyes aren't enough, and how to check

video.title: Deepfakes and AI-made content
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher, Nigeria, the student's teacher (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher, the student's teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Cards: A famous footballer; “Free airtime!”; Shared by half the class.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Last week a video went round our class group. A famous footballer promised free airtime to anyone who shared a link. It was fake, and half the class had already shared it.

scenes.visual: The title card: the course, the lesson title and subtitle, the Darsi mark.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how AI fakes are made, why your eyes aren't enough, and how to check.

scenes.visual: A list: Face swap: a new face; Lip-sync: new words; Voice copy: from a short clip.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A deepfake is a photo, video or voice made or changed by AI to look real. Face swapping puts one face on another body. Lip-syncing makes a mouth say new words. And a voice can be copied from a short clip.

scenes.visual: A table: the old clues (odd hands, blurry teeth, a robot voice) are each fixed by new tools; the last row, a fake with no mistakes at all, can still be fake.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: You may know the old clues: odd hands, blurry teeth, a robot voice. They help sometimes. But new tools fix them, so a fake with no mistakes can still be fake.

scenes.visual: Cards: Who made it?; Where's the original?; Trusted reports?; Check the story.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: You already know three questions: who made it, where is the original, and do trusted sources report it? Now let's answer them like a fact-checker. Check the story, not just the picture.

scenes.visual: Numbered steps: Check the account; Search for the original; Find a trusted report; Ask who gains.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: First, the account: is it new, or copying a famous name? Second, the original: a reverse image search shows where a picture appeared first. Third, a trusted news site or official page. Fourth, who gains if you believe it?

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A clip shows our head teacher saying school is closed tomorrow. It's on a new account with no other posts. What do you do?

scenes.visual: A list: The school's own channel; A new account: a warning sign; Forwarding spreads it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Check the real channel first: the school's notice board, its official page, or your teacher. A new account with no history is a warning sign. And forwarding it, even to ask, helps it spread.

scenes.visual: A table of what a watermark detector says: watermarked text is flagged; honest writing is sometimes flagged; watermarked text after a few edits is missed.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: What about AI detectors? Some tools hide a watermark in what they make, or add an “AI-made” label. A detector looks for those signs. But it gives a chance, not proof: honest work gets flagged, and edits wipe the signal.

scenes.visual: Cards joined by arrows: Write with a watermark; The detector flags it; Change a few words; Flag gone.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: In the app, write with a hidden watermark and watch the detector flag it. Then change a few words, and watch the flag disappear. And notice when an honest sentence gets flagged by chance.

scenes.visual: A list: A fake of a classmate; Spreads in minutes; Never make or share one.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Some fakes are made to hurt people. A fake photo of a classmate can spread in minutes. Making or sharing one is never a joke, and in many countries it's a crime.

scenes.visual: The quick check: the question and its answer cards, with the speaker beside them.
scenes.animation: The speaker slides in; answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Someone posts a fake picture of you in a group chat. What's the best first step?

scenes.visual: The summary: Targeted? Save, report, tell; Check the story, not the glitches; Detectors are clues, not proof; Never make or share fakes. Takeaway: Pause, check the real source, then decide.
scenes.animation: Points tick in as they are said; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Story · Clues · Never share · Get help
scenes.narration: Save evidence, report it, and tell an adult you trust. Remember: glitches don't last, so check the story. Detectors are clues, not proof. And never make or share a fake of a real person.

scenes.visual: A list: Pick one viral post; Check the account; Find the original; Share what you found, kindly.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: pick one picture or clip going round your family or class group. Check the account, search for the original, and look for a trusted report. Then tell the group what you found, kindly, without forwarding it.

checkpoints.prompt: A clip shows your head teacher saying school is closed tomorrow. It's on a new account with no other posts. What do you do?

options.text: Check the school's real channel before sharing anything
Look closely: if the face looks real, it is real

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Right: check the school's real channel first. Sharing it, even to ask, spreads it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a real-looking face proves nothing, and asking in the group still spreads it.

checkpoints.prompt: Someone posts a fake picture of you in a group chat. What's the best first step?

options.text: Post an angry reply in the group
Save evidence, report it, and tell an adult you trust
Pay them to take it down

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Yes: keep a screenshot, report it in the app, and get help. You don't have to face it alone.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: an angry reply or a payment can make it worse. Save evidence, report it, tell an adult.
